Sedimentation created by reduced flows would reduce the area available to trout for spawning as well as to aquatic insects that represent the major portion of the diet of Howard Creek trout. This impact would be greatest in the reach of Howard Creek immediately below the confluence with Bad Creek. Langdon et al. (1976) found that most of the sediment transport in Howard Creek occurs during high flow periods. Thus, the reduction in normal flow may not have a great impact on the ability of this stream to transport sediments. Significant reductions in storm flows could adversely affect sedimentation and sediment transport. These authors noted that Howard Creek appears to have the capacity to remove suspended sediments, but coarser materials comprising the bed load fraction could be a problem.
Applicant has estimated that seepage from the upper reservoir would be as much as 5 cfs and may serve as a source of high quality supplemental water to Howard Creek to mitigate the loss from impoundment of Bad Creek and West Bad Creek. Applicant states that this water would be "relatively natural spring-like water at groundwater temperatures." (Exhibit W, Amendment 1, Pg. W 3-12). This seepage would make a negligible contribution to storm flows, but could add significantly to base flows (Langdon, et al., 1976). The seepage flows contributed to Howard Creek would not approach the natural seasonal flow cycle expected under normal conditions. Stream communities would benefit during low flow periods, if the 5 cfs seepage flow was maintained throughout the year as predicted.
Applicant proposes to construct a flow augmentation system with a multilevel intake at the upper reservoir. The intake levels would be at elevations 2,280 feet, 2,230 feet, and 2,120 feet msl (30 feet, 80 feet, and 190 feet below full pool elevation, respectively) with discharge through an aeration device at the base of the Bad Creek Dam. The intake located at elevation 2,120 feet would be about 30 feet below maximum drawdown. The augmentation system would be capable of delivering flows of up to 15 cfs, an amount that would more than restore Howard Creek to preproject base flow levels.
